newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Remote Russian Far East city makes U.S. ice cream.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Remote Russian Far East city makes U.S. ice cream.

text.p: In December, a state inspector looked over Frank's Siberian Supreme, a tiny operation trying to make American ice cream for an isolated corner of the Russian Far East, and decided their documents were not in order.

"At first I thought it was a joke, but she was powerful enough to close us down," said Alexei Rekounov, the company's 24-year-old sales manager. "In this country a clerk is everything. An official is tsar and king."
The suspension that resulted was just one of many obstacles the company, started with $150,000 from an American businessman, has had in opening up small-scale ice cream production.

Even today, a year and a half after they began operations, only a few stores sell Siberian Supreme's tasty versions of peach, strawberry, cherry and chocolate in Magadan, a regional centre 8,000 km (5,000 miles) east of Moscow.

"In the beginning, we had problems with quality because we had no experience," said Andranik Mirtitsyan, 25, the company's Russian director who wears a leather jacket, thin sweat pants, and a trim crewcut.

Frank Edgerly, the California partner whose name adorns each carton of the ice cream, added: "We've had every problem you could think of...There are many times I asked myself why I am trying to make ice cream."
MODEST PRODUCTION FACILITIES
Even today, the mini-factory with four workers in the space of a large apartment lined with linoleum flooring looks more like a hastily improvised operation than ice cream wonderland.

One room holds bags of American ice cream powder, another a modern ice cream machine where they mix in filtered local water, and two contain freezers for the final product. The office has a portrait of Lenin with a Siberian Supreme sticker on his lapel and a Playboy centerfold posted nearby.

The grassroots venture started when Edgerly, 32, who was involved in timber and food export businesses with Russia, travelled to Magadan to help build a church and met the young men who today staff Siberian Supreme.
"We figured we could make ice cream quite a bit cheaper than importing it pre-made," he said in an telephone interview.

Since then the idea has attracted the attention of the American government-funded U.S.-Russia Investment Fund, which is finalising a deal to buy 40 percent of Siberian Supreme for $300,000, company officials said.

"We're looking at making a direct investment to help the company," said Derek Norberg, head of the U.S.-Russia Investment Fund in the Far East. "You have a unique situation in Magadan because there is no local production. Because it's cut off from land routes, any local production does have an advantage."

Operating in a small market has distinct pluses. The 30- second television commercial they recently prepared costs less than $20 to air eight times a day locally. And in a city where the severe northern climate and isolation from Russian ground shipping routes limit the variety of food, ice cream becomes especially alluring at the dining table.
Even the unusually cold local weather -- locals wear jackets against brisk winds even in July, and winter temperatures can fall to -60 C (-76 Fahrenheit) -- is no deterrent.
"The colder the territory, the more people eat ice cream," said Rekounov.
FIGHTING BUREAUCRATS, COMPETITORS
Siberian Supreme is now producing only 150-200 cartons a day, which brings them a profit of about $1 a carton. And their encounter with Russian-style bureaucracy has left the staff a bit scarred.
"It's pretty hard, mostly because of the regulations," Rekounov said. "We have many enemies among bureaucrats who want to trip us up."
Anna Konovich, the city's main state inspector on food quality, said Siberian Supreme was closed for two months because it failed to provide required documentation.

"If it's not done with our technology, we need an explanation in our documentation," she said. "But they didn't have any documents, the date of expiration wasn't clear, and neither was who made the product."
In addition to fighting back state bureaucrats, the firm is far behind a local importer, Amros, which has been shipping in Wells' Blue Bunny ice cream from Iowa to local stores.
"We don't see them even as competitors, because people are already used to Blue Bunny," said Amros sales manager Mikhail Gerasimovich.

He said Amros delivers three containers with 6,000 to 8,000 individual cartons of ice cream a month to the port city first established as a gateway to Stalin's Gulag system of prison camps in the 1930s.
Edgerly said he is soon bringing in display cases for Magadan stores and plans to pump up production significantly to expand his market share.
He added he is undaunted by the experience of American ice cream maker Ben & Jerry's, which pulled out of Russia earlier this year after deciding their high-profile joint venture was not paying off.
In fact, Siberian Supreme officials are confident they will soon expand to other cities in the Russian Far East, and then into Siberia.
"Magadan is only the beginning," Mirtitsyan said. "If it works here, it should work easily elsewhere."
